title: Strategy and Template Method
goal: By the end you can pass algorithms as lambdas and comparators, refactor an if/else pricer into a strategy map or an exhaustive switch behind a characterization test, and replace a Template Method base class with an execute-around function.
opening:
Every parcel leaves the corner shop the same way: weigh it, choose a courier, book it, print the label. Only the choosing changes. Most days the shopkeeper picks the cheapest courier, for an urgent order the fastest, and in heavy rain the van. Down the road, the bakery's bread recipe card has fixed steps (mix, knead, shape, bake, cool) and one blank, the shape, which changes with every loaf.

Code has both shapes: a routine with one decision plugged in, and a recipe with one step left open. The easy traps are an `if`/`else` chain that grows a branch for every new way to deliver, and a base class that asks for its blank before anyone has filled it in.

In the last lesson, we arranged objects into trees and bridges. In this lesson, we'll pass one decision in as a lambda (Strategy), refactor an `if`/`else` pricer without changing a cent, leave a blank for a subclass (Template Method), and then fill it with a function instead. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.

warmup.q: Delivery prices are worked out two ways: through an `EnumMap<DeliveryMethod, PriceStrategy>`, and through a `switch` expression over `DeliveryMethod` with no `default`. A teammate adds `DRONE` to the `DeliveryMethod` enum and builds. What happens?
options: Both versions fail to compile
The switch fails to compile; the map compiles and throws on the first drone parcel
The map fails to compile; the switch throws at runtime
Both compile, and drone parcels cost 0
warmup.why: A switch expression over an enum with no `default` must cover every constant, so javac reports "the switch expression does not cover all possible input values" right where the rule is missing. The map has no idea which keys should exist: `EnumMap.get(DRONE)` returns null, and calling `priceCents` on it throws when the program runs. That difference decides which shape fits which job, as the second section shows.

sections.h: Strategy: the one decision you pass in
sections.body:
Back to the shop counter. The routine for sending a parcel stays the same, and one decision inside it is swapped: which courier to use. The rule for that decision can change from order to order without touching the rest of the routine.

Java's `sort` works the same way. It owns the routine for putting a list in order and leaves one decision to you, passed in as an object: which of two items goes first. That object is a **comparator**, and it's the Strategy pattern in one line. A **strategy** is one interchangeable algorithm, passed in by the caller and used by the code that needs the decision. That code is called the **context**.

In *Design Patterns*, the 1994 book that named these patterns, a strategy meant an interface and a class for every algorithm. Since Java 8, a lambda or a method reference is the class. Here the shop ranks courier quotes, each with a price and a delivery time:

```java
record Quote(String courier, long priceCents, long minutes) {}

Comparator<Quote> cheapest = Comparator.comparingLong(Quote::priceCents);
Comparator<Quote> cheapestThenFastest = cheapest.thenComparingLong(Quote::minutes);

quotes.sort(cheapestThenFastest);           // sort is the context; the comparator is the strategy
```

```kotlin
data class Quote(val courier: String, val priceCents: Long, val minutes: Long)

val cheapest = compareBy<Quote> { it.priceCents }
val cheapestThenFastest = cheapest.thenBy { it.minutes }

val ordered = quotes.sortedWith(cheapestThenFastest)   // sortedWith is the context; the comparator is the strategy
```

`Comparator.comparing` "accepts a function that extracts a Comparable sort key" and returns a comparator. `thenComparing` chains a second comparator behind it, used only when the first one ties. Nobody writes a class called `PriceThenTimeComparator` any more. Kotlin's `compareBy` and `thenBy` do the same with function types, and any `(Parcel) -> Long` already is a pricing strategy, with no interface to declare.

`StrategyDemo`, in the Try it, ranks three quotes three ways. They come from Pedal Post, Big Blue Vans and Kestrel, a new courier in town:

```text
cheapest: [Big Blue Vans, Pedal Post, Kestrel]
fastest: [Kestrel, Pedal Post, Big Blue Vans]
cheapest, then fastest: [Big Blue Vans, Kestrel, Pedal Post]
```

Look at the first line. Pedal Post and Kestrel both cost 4.50, and they stay in the order they came in, because the JDK's sort is **stable**: it never swaps two items that compare equal. The third strategy breaks that tie by time, so Kestrel's 20 minutes beat Pedal Post's 30.

The JDK hands you strategies in more places than sorting. A `ThreadPoolExecutor`, the JDK's pool of worker threads, takes a `RejectedExecutionHandler` that decides what happens when its queue is full. `Collectors.groupingBy` takes the function that decides which group each element joins. Each time, the library owns the loop and asks you for one decision.

A named type still helps in two cases. When the strategy has more than one method, such as a courier client with `book` and `track`, you have an interface with implementations, which is ordinary polymorphism: one interface, several classes, one of them chosen while the program runs. And a one-line `@FunctionalInterface interface PriceStrategy { long priceCents(Parcel p); }` says more than a bare `ToLongFunction<Parcel>`, and reads better in stack traces, the list of calls an exception prints.

The counter picture breaks on memory. The shopkeeper remembers that yesterday's van was late. A strategy shouldn't remember anything. A lambda that captures and changes a field is a strategy with hidden memory, a shopkeeper still holding a grudge, and two threads sorting with it at once will corrupt each other's results.

**A strategy is one decision, passed in. Keep it pure: input in, answer out.**

A comparator is a strategy for a context someone else wrote. Next, a context of our own that grew the old way.

compare.title: An execute-around timer for a courier library

java.title: Couriers.java

kotlin.title: Couriers.kt

compare.note: The recipe is identical: read the clock, run the caller's block, record in `finally`. Three things differ. Java's standard functional interfaces can't throw checked exceptions, so a library that throws `IOException` forces you to declare `IoCall` with a `throws` clause; Kotlin has no checked exceptions. Kotlin's `inline` copies `timed` and the block into each call site, so there is no lambda object, and `return null` inside the block returns from `bookOrNull` itself while the `finally` still runs. And an inline block may call suspend functions when the caller is a suspend function, which a Java lambda can't do. Neither language needs Template Method for this; the function is the whole pattern.

worked.title: Turn a back-off if/else into strategies, without changing behavior

steps.say: When a courier's line is busy, the shop's retry helper waits a little before trying again; that wait is called the back-off. The helper reads the back-off rule's name from the settings file and decides the wait on every attempt. Spot two problems before reading on.

The rule is chosen again on every attempt, and a typo like `doubeling` quietly becomes "fixed". Fix neither yet. First pin today's behavior with a characterization test, so the refactor can't change a wait by accident.
Now give the decision a type with one method, and a factory for each rule. Each factory returns a lambda: a complete strategy.

Choose the strategy once, at startup. Here a `default` is right, because names in a settings file are an open set you don't control, and it throws, so a typo stops the program the moment it starts. Point the pinned test at `fromSettings(policy).delay(attempt)`: it still passes.
steps.alt_code:
fun fromSettings(name: String): Backoff = when (name) {                 // 2. choose once, at startup
    "fixed" -> Backoff.fixed(Duration.ofMillis(200))
    "doubling" -> Backoff.doubling(Duration.ofMillis(100), Duration.ofSeconds(5))
    "none" -> Backoff.NONE
    else -> throw IllegalArgumentException("unknown courier.backoff: $name") // 3. a typo stops the start
}

val backoff = fromSettings(settings.backoff)                             // 4. the retry loop calls backoff.delay(n)

lab.title: Refactor the delivery pricer twice, and replace a template with a function
steps: Read `DeliveryMethod`, `Parcel` and `LegacyPricer`. They are given, and `LegacyPricer.priceCents` is the specification. Run the tests: all eight fail.

Write `DeliveryPrices.strategies()`: a `new EnumMap<>(DeliveryMethod.class)` with one lambda per method. Copy the rules from `LegacyPricer`, including the hill surcharge outside the Old Town. Then write `priceByMap` as one line.
Write `priceBySwitch` as a switch expression over `p.method()` with no `default`.
Write `Outbound.timed`: one clock read before, the body in a `try`, the outcome noted in a `catch` that rethrows, one record added in `finally`. Compare it with the given `OutboundCall`.
Run the tests until all eight pass. Then add `DRONE` to `DeliveryMethod` and build: which of your two refactors complains? Remove it again.
hints: For the bike, `200 + p.grams() * 30 / 1_000 + (p.district().equals("Old Town") ? 0 : p.grams() * 10 / 1_000)`. Keep the two divisions separate, exactly as the legacy code has them, or the parity test finds the cent: 999 g outside the Old Town is 238, not 239.
`Comparator.comparingLong(Quote::priceCents).thenComparingLong(Quote::minutes).thenComparing(Quote::courier)` sorts by price, then time, then name.

Declare `String outcome = "ok";` before the `try`, set it to `e.getClass().getSimpleName()` in `catch (RuntimeException e)`, rethrow with `throw e;`, and add the `CallRecord` in `finally`, so success and failure each log exactly once.

alt.title: Kotlin

recap: Strategy is an algorithm the caller picks and passes in. In modern Java and Kotlin, a lambda, a method reference or a function type is the strategy; `Comparator.comparing` is the JDK's own example.
Before refactoring an `if`/`else` chain, pin its behavior with a characterization test over a grid of edge inputs, such as weight 0, weight 1 and 999 g.

Use a map of strategies for open sets (settings, plug-ins) and a `switch` or `when` with no default for closed sets you own. A missing map entry fails when the program runs; a missing case fails to compile.
Template Method is a final recipe in a base class with hooks for subclasses. Never call a hook from a constructor: the subclass's fields are still unset, even Kotlin non-null `val`s.

Execute around replaces most Template Methods: the recipe is a function and the changing step is a lambda, as in try-with-resources, `use`, `synchronized` and `measureTimeMillis`. Kotlin `inline` makes it free of lambda objects.

The limit: a passed-in function swaps one decision or one step, not the order of the steps. When what may happen next depends on what happened before, you need something that remembers, which is where lesson 9 of this track goes.
closing:
We started with a shopkeeper choosing a courier and a recipe card with one blank. The choice became a comparator or a lambda passed in, and the long `if`/`else` became a map or a switch, pinned by a test against the old code. The blank became a hook, and then simply a function's parameter.

Now look in your own code for a base class whose constructor calls an abstract or open method. Each one hands its subclasses a half-built object.

Next, we'll tell everyone who cares that something happened, and turn a request into a slip of paper. How does the shop ring a bell for everyone who signed up, without knowing who they are?

quiz.q: A team prices with `Map<DeliveryMethod, PriceStrategy>` built from settings, and also has a `switch` over `DeliveryMethod` with no default in the receipt code. Someone adds `DRONE` to `DeliveryMethod`. Which statement is true?
options: The map fails to compile; the switch throws at runtime
The switch fails to compile; the map compiles and fails on the first drone parcel
Both fail to compile
Both compile, and drone parcels cost 0
quiz.why: Only the switch tells the compiler which constants must be handled, so only the switch breaks the build. The map has no idea `DRONE` should be a key, so `get` returns null when the program runs. With a map over a closed set, add a check at startup that every constant has an entry.

quiz.q: Quotes: Hilltop Couriers (price 300, 40 minutes), Gull Express (price 250, 75 minutes), Riverside Bikes (price 300, 25 minutes), in that order. In what order does `Comparator.comparingLong(Quote::priceCents).thenComparingLong(Quote::minutes)` sort them?
options: Gull Express, Riverside Bikes, Hilltop Couriers
Gull Express, Hilltop Couriers, Riverside Bikes
Riverside Bikes, Hilltop Couriers, Gull Express
Hilltop Couriers, Riverside Bikes, Gull Express
quiz.why: The first comparator puts the 250 price first: Gull Express. Hilltop and Riverside tie on price, so the second comparator breaks the tie by time: Riverside's 25 minutes before Hilltop's 40. The tempting "Gull Express, Hilltop Couriers, Riverside Bikes" ignores the tie-breaker and keeps the original order.

quiz.q: A base class sets `label = "outbound " + name();` in its constructor. The subclass `BookingCall(String courier)` assigns `this.courier = courier` and implements `name()` as `"booking via " + courier`. What is the label of `new BookingCall("Pedal Post")`?
options: It throws `NullPointerException`
`outbound booking via Pedal Post`
`outbound booking via null`
It doesn't compile
quiz.why: The base constructor runs first and calls the overridden `name()` before `BookingCall` has assigned `courier`, so `courier` is still null, and string concatenation turns null into "null". Nothing throws, which makes the bug easy to miss. Kotlin behaves the same even for a non-null `val courier: String`.

quiz.q: At 30 places, the shop's code calls different courier services, and every call must be timed and logged in the same way. Which shape fits best?
options: An abstract base class with a final `execute()` and one subclass per call site
A `Map<String, Runnable>` holding all 30 calls
A singleton that every call registers with
A higher-order function, `timed("courier.book") { ... }`, `inline` in Kotlin, wrapped around each call
quiz.why: The steps around the call are fixed and the middle changes per call site, which is execute around: one function, and each call site passes its own block. Thirty subclasses is Template Method's ceremony with its inheritance problems, and a map or a singleton doesn't wrap anything.

quiz.q: From *Decorator and Proxy*: each delivery method's base rule is a `DeliveryFee` stored in a `Map<DeliveryMethod, DeliveryFee>`. The shop now wants every delivery capped at 8.00. Where does the cap go with the least code?
options: Edit every lambda in the map to call `Math.min(..., 800)`
Decorate each fee once when you build the map: `fees.replaceAll((m, f) -> f.cappedAt(800))`
Add a `default -> 800` branch to the switch
Make each strategy extend a `CappedFee` base class
quiz.why: Strategies and decorators combine: the map picks the rule, and wrapping each rule in `cappedAt(800)` adds the cap once, in one place. Editing every lambda copies the rule into each strategy, a `default` branch changes nothing for known methods, and a base class brings back the inheritance this lesson moves away from.

flashcards.front: In modern Java or Kotlin, what is a strategy usually written as?
flashcards.back: A lambda or method reference for a functional interface (`Comparator`, `PriceStrategy`), or a Kotlin function type such as `(Parcel) -> Long`.

flashcards.front: You add a constant to an enum. What happens to a `switch` over it with no default, and to an `EnumMap` of strategies?
flashcards.back: The switch fails to compile. The map compiles, and `get` returns null for the new key when the program runs.

flashcards.front: Map of strategies or exhaustive switch: which for a closed set you own?
flashcards.back: The switch (or `when`) with no default, so a new case is a compile error. Use the map for open sets: settings, plug-ins.
A test that records what existing code does today, bugs included, so a refactor can prove it changed nothing.
A final recipe method in a base class that calls hook methods subclasses override.

flashcards.front: A base-class constructor calls an overridden method that reads a subclass field. What does it see?
flashcards.back: The field's default: null or 0, because the subclass constructor hasn't run yet. In Kotlin even a non-null `val` reads as null.
A function that runs the steps before and after, and takes the changing step as a lambda: try-with-resources, `use {}`, `synchronized(lock) {}`.

terms.plain: One interchangeable algorithm, passed in by the caller and used by the code that needs a decision.
A test that pins down what old code does now, so a refactor can't change it unnoticed.
A base-class method that fixes the steps and lets subclasses fill in some of them.
An overridable method a template calls at a fixed point in its recipe.
When a change inside a parent class breaks subclasses that relied on how it worked.
A function that wraps the caller's code with steps before and after, taking that code as a lambda.
A Kotlin function whose body, with its lambda arguments, is copied into each place that calls it.

explain_back.prompt: A teammate asks: "Should our delivery prices live in a `Map<DeliveryMethod, PriceStrategy>` or in a `switch` over `DeliveryMethod`?" Explain how you decide, and what each version does on the day someone adds a new way to deliver.
explain_back.answer: It depends on who owns the set of keys. If the set is closed and ours, like the `DeliveryMethod` enum, I use a switch (or `when`) with no default. When someone adds `DRONE`, the build fails at every switch that needs a rule, so nobody can ship without deciding what a drone delivery costs. If the set is open, because rules come from settings or plug-ins or customers switch them on, a map of strategies fits, since the code can't know the keys when it's compiled. The map's weakness is that a missing entry only shows up when the program runs: `EnumMap.get` returns null and the first drone parcel fails. If we use a map for an enum anyway, we add a check at startup that every constant has an entry, so the program refuses to start instead of failing a customer's order. Either way, I'd pin the current prices with a characterization test against the old code before changing anything.

deeper.body:
Strategy and State have the same structure: an object holds an interface and hands the decision to it. The difference is who chooses. The caller picks a strategy, and it stays put. A state object picks the next state itself as things happen to it. Lesson 9 of this track, *State and Chain of Responsibility*, builds that kind of object.

Java can do execute around without lambdas. Make the step before a constructor and the step after `close()`, and try-with-resources does the rest: `try (var t = timings.start("courier.book")) { return courier.book(address, grams); }`. This form lets checked exceptions pass through untouched and needs no functional interface, which is why many timing and logging libraries offer a closeable timer. The cost is that the caller must remember the `try`.

Kotlin's `inline` has limits worth knowing. An inlined lambda can't be stored or passed to a function that isn't inline, because it doesn't exist as an object; mark such a parameter `noinline`. If the lambda runs somewhere else, such as on another thread or in a callback, mark it `crossinline`, which forbids a `return` from the outer function inside it. And large inline functions grow every place that calls them, so keep them small: the recipe inline, the heavy lifting in a normal function it calls.

Strategies hide in Kotlin's collection functions too. `sortedWith`, `maxByOrNull { it.priceCents }`, `groupBy { it.method }` and `partition { it.grams > 5_000 }` each own the loop and take one decision from you as a lambda.
